parts: Business activities fall into two broad groups: industry, which is concerned with producing goods, and commerce, which is concerned with distributing them to those who need them. So Business = Industry + Commerce.

Industry is the production side of business — raising, producing, processing or manufacturing goods. Its products are consumer goods (used finally by consumers — food grains, textiles, cosmetics) or producer goods (used to make other goods — machinery, tools). The word also means a group of factories making the same product (cement industry, cotton textile industry).

(1) Primary industry: production with the help of nature, needing little human effort — agriculture, forestry, fishing, horticulture.
(2) Genetic industry: reproducing and multiplying certain species of plants and animals for sale — plant nurseries, cattle breeding, poultry.
(3) Extractive industry: drawing out goods from the soil, air or water; products are usually raw materials for other industries — mining, coal, oil, iron ore, extraction of timber and rubber from forests.
(4) Manufacturing industry: converting raw materials into finished goods with machines and manpower — textiles, chemicals, sugar, paper, oil refining.
(5) Construction industry: building houses, roads, bridges, dams, canals — goods are erected at one place, not moved.
(6) Service industry: providing services — hotels, tourism, entertainment.
Commerce: trade and aids to trade

Commerce covers all the activities needed for a free, uninterrupted flow of goods from producers to consumers. It includes trade and aids to trade. Trade means buying and selling. A wholesaler buys in large quantities from producers and sells in smaller lots to retailers; a retailer buys from wholesalers (or producers) and sells in small quantities to the final consumers. Aids (auxiliaries) to trade remove the hindrances to trade: transport (place — land, water, air), warehousing (time — storage until sold), insurance (risk — compensation for loss by fire, theft, accident), advertising (information — creates demand; indoor such as newspapers, radio, TV, and outdoor such as hoardings and posters) and banking (finance — deposits, loans, payment services).

E-commerce (electronic commerce) means buying, selling and exchanging goods and services over computer networks such as the Internet, with transactions completed electronically. Online retail selling is called e-tailing. Compared with traditional business, e-business is easy to form, needs no physical presence, costs less to set up and run, takes less time per transaction, has a shorter business cycle, gets more government help and has a much wider (global) reach — but offers less personal touch.

Types of e-commerce: B2B (business-to-business — a manufacturer sending quotations to or selling to distributors, wholesalers to retailers; prices often negotiable on quantity); B2C (business-to-consumer — online stores selling to the public); C2B (consumer-to-business — a consumer posts a project with a budget and companies bid; it empowers consumers to invite bids); C2C (consumer-to-consumer — classifieds and auctions such as eBay). Others: B2E, G2B, G2C, etc.

Advantages of e-commerce: wider choice for customers and a wider (even global) market for sellers; improved customer service before and after the sale; quick response to customer needs because the distribution channel is cut short; cost saving and lower prices (no showrooms, fewer godowns and employees); access to market information to identify customer needs; business round the clock.
